key_terms.meaning: On-board computer that stores the flight plan, predicts time and fuel, and sends steering commands to the autopilot; chapter 1.
FMS file of waypoints, airways, navaids and airport data from which the flight plan is built; chapter 1.
A rule that turns target information (bearing, range, LOS angle) into an acceleration command; chapter 2.
The straight line joining the missile (or launcher) to the target; chapter 2.
Rate of change of the LOS angle, in rad/s; a hit needs λ̇ → 0 at intercept; chapter 2.
Guidance computer stays on the ground or launcher and sends steering commands to the missile by radio; chapter 3.
Seeker and guidance computer travel inside the missile, so it steers itself; chapter 3.
Sensor head (radar, infrared or imaging) that measures the target direction from the missile; chapter 3.
Missile nose is kept pointed at the target, so the velocity vector aims at the current target position; chapter 4.
Command to line-of-sight: the missile is held on the line from launcher to target; chapter 4.
Acceleration command a = N·V_c·λ̇ applied normal to the LOS; chapter 5.
Dimensionless gain of proportional navigation, normally 3 to 5; chapter 5.
PN plus a target-acceleration term, a = N·V_c·λ̇ + (N/2)·a_T; chapter 5.
Actuator and gearbox that turn a small guidance command into a fin deflection angle; chapter 6.
Pitch and yaw fins produce lateral acceleration while the airframe stays nearly level; chapter 6.
Control loop that holds the missile steady about its long axis and rejects roll disturbances; chapter 7.
Loop that converts a yaw or pitch acceleration command into the fin deflection that produces it; chapter 7.
The whole airframe rolls so that its lift vector points in the required turn direction; chapter 7.
Spinning wheel on a spacecraft; speeding it up or slowing it down torques the body the other way; chapter 8.
Insulation, surface coatings, heaters and radiators that keep every unit inside its temperature limits; chapter 8.

takeaways: A guidance law is only a mapping from measured target information to an acceleration command; everything else is hardware that must deliver that command.
The four guidance families are command, homing, navigation (terrain or stellar referenced) and hybrid; the choice is set by where the computer sits and what sensor it can see.
Pursuit and CLOS look simple but leave a non-zero LOS rate at intercept, so the miss distance grows quickly against a crossing target.
Proportional navigation drives the LOS rate to zero by commanding a = N·V_c·λ̇, which is why it is the default law in most missiles.
The PN variants differ only in the reference frame of the measurement and in whether target acceleration is estimated: PPN, TPN, APN, TPN, GPN, IPN.
The autopilot, fin servo and airframe dynamics sit inside the guidance loop, so slow or saturating fins turn a good law into a large miss distance.
A bank-to-turn airframe turns by rolling first, which gives it more lift for a given angle of attack but slows the response and couples the axes.
A spacecraft cannot refuel or open a window, so power, thermal and attitude control must all work from stored energy and radiation alone.
bank_note: Long answers lean on the classical guidance laws — deriving and comparing the PN variants, LOS-rate reasoning, miss-distance argument — plus the roll/lateral autopilot and fin-servo chain, with the FMS and spacecraft subsystems usually asked as shorter parts.

bank.q: Define a guidance law and describe the four families of guidance laws, giving one practical example of each.
outline: Definition: rule mapping target information to an acceleration command
Family 1: command guidance — computer on ground or launcher
Family 2: homing guidance — computer inside missile, seeker data
Family 3: navigation guidance — inertial, stellar, terrain reference
Family 4: hybrid and modern laws — combined or optimal
One real example per family, with the sensor each needs

bank.q: Compare command guidance with homing guidance: block diagrams, information flow, accuracy, jamming and cost.
outline: Command: target tracked by ground radar, missile tracked too, steering sent by radio uplink
Homing: seeker in the missile, no uplink needed after launch
Command needs a datalink and a ground radar; homing needs an expensive seeker
Homing accuracy falls with seeker noise and radome error; command accuracy falls with tracking error and link delay
Command suits short-range or beam-riding systems; homing suits fire-and-forget
Jamming and countermeasure behaviour of each

bank.q: State the main functions of a flight management system and trace how a flight plan entered by the crew becomes a steering command at the autopilot.
outline: Navigation: position from IRS, GPS, radio navaids, Kalman blending
Flight planning: route from navigation database, waypoints, legs, constraints
Performance: fuel, time, climb and descent profile prediction
Guidance: cross-track and vertical deviation turned into roll and pitch commands
Autopilot and flight director follow the command; autothrottle follows the speed target
Crew interface, datalink uplink of routes, alerting

bank.q: Explain pursuit guidance and CLOS guidance with sketches. Why does each of them fail to bring the line-of-sight rate to zero against a crossing target?
outline: Pursuit: missile velocity vector points at the target at every instant
Pure pursuit gives a tail chase with ever-growing lateral demand; lag pursuit and lead pursuit as variants
CLOS: missile held on the launcher–target line by a beam or radio command
Both leave a non-zero LOS rate for a crossing target, so the missile must keep turning
Acceleration demand grows without limit near intercept; miss distance grows with target speed
Effect of missile speed advantage and of range

bank.q: Describe the power, thermal and attitude control subsystems of a spacecraft and explain why each must work without a pilot.
outline: Power: solar array, battery, shunt or converter regulation, distribution and load switching
Thermal: insulation blankets, coatings, radiators, heaters, heat pipes, temperature limits of units
Attitude: sensors (sun, star, horizon, gyro), actuators (reaction wheels, thrusters, magnetic torquers), control loop
Why autonomy: light-time delay, no atmosphere, no maintenance, long mission life
Fault detection and safe modes
Momentum dumping and orbit keeping

bank.q: A missile closing on its target at V_c = 900 m/s measures a line-of-sight rate of 0.02 rad/s. Using pure proportional navigation with N = 4, find the commanded lateral acceleration in m/s² and in g.
outline: State the law a = N·V_c·λ̇ with every symbol defined
Substitute: a = 4 × 900 × 0.02 = 72 m/s²
Convert: 72 / 9.81 ≈ 7.3 g
Direction: normal to the LOS, in the sense that reduces λ̇
Comment on saturation if the airframe cannot supply 7.3 g
Comment on the effect of raising N to 5

bank.q: A target manoeuvres normal to the line of sight at 6 g. With N = 4, compute the extra acceleration that augmented proportional navigation demands over pure PN, and explain why the extra term is needed.
outline: APN law: a = N·V_c·λ̇ + (N/2)·a_T
Extra term = (N/2)·a_T = 2 × 6 g = 12 g
Pure PN only reacts after λ̇ has already built up
Against a manoeuvring target PN leaves a steady-state lag and a residual miss
Cost: target acceleration a_T must be estimated, usually from seeker data
TPN and other variants that avoid needing a_T

bank.q: A bank-to-turn missile needs a lateral acceleration of 10 g. Its pitch demand is 6 g and its yaw demand is 8 g. Find the roll angle command and the total normal acceleration, and explain the steps the autopilot takes.
outline: Resolve the demand into body pitch and yaw components
Magnitude = √(6² + 8²) = 10 g; roll angle φ = arctan(8/6) ≈ 53°
Roll autopilot drives the airframe to φ using roll fins or ailerons
Then only pitch command is applied; the lift vector does the turning
Advantages: one strong lift direction, less drag, better for ramjet intakes
Penalties: roll must finish before the turn, cross-coupling, slower response

bank.q: A guidance command from the seeker must reach the fin as a deflection angle in a few milliseconds. Describe the fin actuation servo chain, and explain how servo bandwidth, gear ratio, deadband and rate limit affect the guidance loop.
outline: Chain: command → servo amplifier → motor (electric, hydraulic or pneumatic) → gearbox → fin
Position feedback from a potentiometer or resolver; rate feedback for damping
Bandwidth must be well above the airframe natural frequency and the guidance loop crossover
Gear ratio trades fin torque against fin speed
Deadband causes limit cycles and a steady miss; rate limit causes phase lag under large commands
Stall and hinge moment limits under high dynamic pressure

bank.q: Compare pursuit, CLOS and proportional navigation in terms of the line-of-sight rate each produces, the acceleration demanded and the miss distance against a crossing, manoeuvring target.
outline: Define λ̇ and the collision-course condition λ̇ = 0
Pursuit: λ̇ stays finite, demand rises near intercept, tail chase against a receding target
CLOS: missile forced onto the launcher–target line; demand grows with missile range from the line
PN: command proportional to λ̇, so λ̇ is driven to zero; finite and bounded demand
Plot or sketch of acceleration against time for the three laws
Effect of target manoeuvre: all three degrade, PN least

bank.q: A seeker measures LOS rate with noise, the radome adds a boresight error that grows with look angle, and the fin servo has finite bandwidth. Analyse how these three effects together set the miss distance of a PN homing missile.
outline: Guidance loop as a feedback loop with seeker, filter, autopilot, servo, airframe and kinematics
Seeker noise passed through the loop; too high an N amplifies noise into fin demand
Radome slope error creates a parasitic feedback loop that can destabilise the flight path
Servo lag and rate limit add phase lag, reducing gain and phase margin
Miss distance grows with target manoeuvre, with heading error and with loop lag
Design measures: proper N, lead filters, radome compensation, higher servo bandwidth, head pointing

bank.q: Evaluate bank-to-turn against skid-to-turn for an air-to-air missile. Which would you choose for a long-range ramjet missile and why?
outline: STT: separate pitch and yaw fins, airframe stays level, fast independent response
BTT: roll first, then pull; lift vector aligned with the turn
BTT gives more normal force per angle of attack because the whole body lifts
BTT reduces drag and suits ramjet intake orientation and antenna alignment
BTT costs time for the roll and creates roll–yaw–pitch coupling
Choice: BTT for long range with air-breathing propulsion; STT for agility at short range

bank.q: Classical PN uses only LOS rate. Modern guidance laws use optimal control, differential game or sliding-mode ideas. Evaluate what these laws gain and what they demand from the on-board systems.
outline: Classical laws: PPN, TPN, APN, GPN, IPN — simple, need LOS rate and closing velocity
Optimal laws: minimise a cost of miss distance plus control effort; need target model and time-to-go
Differential game laws: assume a smart evading target; give a worst-case guaranteed miss
Sliding-mode and robust laws: tolerate uncertainty but demand fast switching and care with fin rate limits
Costs: more computation, better estimation (time-to-go, target acceleration), more sensors
Practical outcome: PN variants still dominate; modern laws used where a large miss margin is needed

bank.q: An aircraft loses GPS in flight. Analyse how the flight management system keeps navigation and guidance working, and what the crew and autopilot lose.
outline: FMS position normally blended from IRS, GPS and radio navaids by a Kalman filter
Without GPS, IRS-only position drifts with time; radio navaid updates restore it
Navigation database and flight plan remain valid; waypoint sequencing continues
Required navigation performance may no longer be met, so the route or approach must change
Autopilot can still fly headings, tracks and barometric vertical paths
Crew alerting, reversion to conventional navaids, and the case for GNSS-independent backup

glossary.def: On-board computer that holds the flight plan, predicts time and fuel, and gives steering commands to the autopilot.
A named point with known coordinates that the flight plan passes through.
The process of computing and issuing the steering commands that take a vehicle to a target or along a path.
The straight line joining the missile or launcher to the target at any instant.
The angular speed at which the line of sight rotates, measured in rad/s.
A geometry in which the line-of-sight rate stays zero, so missile and target meet if neither manoeuvres.
Guidance in which the computer stays on the ground or launcher and sends steering commands to the missile.
Guidance in which the seeker and computer are inside the missile, so it steers itself after launch.
Guidance in which the missile stays inside a radar or laser beam pointed at the target.
Guidance that keeps the missile velocity vector pointed at the target's current position.
Command to line-of-sight; the missile is forced to stay on the line from launcher to target.
Guidance that commands acceleration proportional to the line-of-sight rate, a = N·V_c·λ̇.
The rate at which the missile–target range decreases, in m/s, written V_c.
The dimensionless gain N in proportional navigation, typically between 3 and 5.
PN with an added term proportional to target acceleration to counter manoeuvres.
The closest approach between missile and target, the main measure of guidance quality.
Control loop that holds or commands the vehicle's attitude and rate of turn.
Motor, gearbox and feedback loop that move a fin to the angle the guidance command asks for.
Control in which pitch and yaw fins turn the missile while the body stays nearly level.
Control in which the missile rolls first so its lift vector points in the direction of the turn.
Apparent shift of target angle caused by the nose dome, which feeds back into the guidance loop as a false LOS rate.
Spinning wheel used to exchange angular momentum with a spacecraft so the body turns.
Removing excess momentum stored in reaction wheels, usually with thrusters or magnetic torquers.
Surface on a spacecraft that dumps waste heat to space by radiation.
Camera that compares star patterns with a catalogue to give the spacecraft's attitude.
The set of coatings, insulation, heaters and radiators that keep units inside their temperature limits.
